transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: Mon Mar 30 2026 14:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Jordan Ruiz (Redwood CSM brief), Oliver Grant (KiteWorks Head of Platform), Maya Singh (KiteWorks SRE), Jon Reyes (Product), Priya Nair (Security)

[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to walk through the SLO handoff for the pilot — TTFT versus TPOT, a quick bit on workload sizing and a measurement plan. Does that agenda look ok?
[00:08] Oliver: Yep sounds good, we mostly want clarity on what success looks like. We've got execs asking for latency targets and also cost impact.
[00:15] Maya: And security questions, but I can quick interrupt later.
[00:18] Liam: Great, we'll do the definitions first, then traffic, then measurement. Quick note: my audio's a bit windy, sorry in advance.
[00:24] Jon: No worries.

[02:05] Liam: So, TTFT — first token time — is basically the wall clock from API accept to the first non-empty token. It's sensitive to model cold paths, compilation, kv cache misses, and network. TPOT is total per-request time to produce entire payload — so depends on output length and per-token latency.
[02:30] Maya: Quick clarifying, you call it TTFT as 'tee-tee-f-t'?
[02:33] Liam: (laughs) Yeah similar, sometimes people say t-t-f-t, but we'll use TTFT. We've seen customers treat TTFT as a user-perceived latency SLO and TPOT as throughput/cost SLO.

[05:10] Oliver: For our use case: primary UX is short chat replies ~12-80 tokens, median ~45 tokens. Occasional long summaries to 600 tokens for export. Our current infra shows p95 around 420ms for first byte and p99 ~900ms on our in-house instances — that's rough.
[05:28] Aisha: Good, helps. For a pilot we typically recommend defining both: TTFT p95 and p99, and TPOT p95/p99 or per-token steady-state averages. Example baseline we've run: TTFT p95 180ms, p99 350ms for a 70-token median load on dedicated clusters. TPOT p95 ~~ 2.2s and p99 ~4.8s for heavy outputs — but that varies with model and quantization.

[07:42] Maya: That delta — your p95 180 vs our 420 — why big? Is it hardware? batching?
[07:48] Liam: It's a mix. Our hosted runs are on optimized kernels, persistent warm processes, and KV caching for repeated prefixes. In-house often has cold starts and different batch policies, plus network egress. Also sequence length distribution affects effective batching.

[09:12] Jon: For the pilot success criteria, would a TTFT p95 target of 300ms and p99 of 700ms be acceptable? That would already look like an improvement for us.
[09:20] Aisha: That's reasonable as a starting acceptance band. For TPOT maybe p95 1.8s and p99 5s for median 45 token replies. We should be explicit about token length buckets — short (<=50), medium (51-200), long (>200).

[11:01] Liam: Measurement plan proposal: we run three phases — baseline (your current infra capture), Redwood dry-run on our staging with your sanitized traffic, and a controlled canary. We'll measure TTFT and TPOT percentiles, plus per-token latency, tokens/sec, KV cache hit-rate, and throughput (RPS).
[11:20] Maya: How many samples do we need for p99 to be statistically meaningful?
[11:25] Liam: Aim for ~100k requests per bucket to get stable p99 with low noise. For p95 you can get away with fewer. That's why we suggested a 4 hour canary with synthetic bursts to capture spikes.

[13:35] Oliver: Workload sizing — our current average QPS for the chat endpoint is 18 steady, peaks to 180 during business hours, and we see short intense spikes up to 450 for ~30-90s. Median concurrency around 12, tail concurrency up to 60. Token distribution: median 45 as said, 95th ~320.
[13:56] Aisha: Great, so for pilot we should test steady 20 RPS, medium 180 RPS sustained for 30m, and spike profiles up to 450 RPS for short bursts. Concurrency targets (threads or workers) we'll map to 60.

[16:10] Jon: Any artificial limits or batching suggestions? We want to keep cost down, so quantization or batching are attractive.
[16:17] Liam: We can run experiments: 8-bit quant, grouped batching windows of 10–30ms to improve throughput. But batching increases TTFT for single request if it waits for group — that's the tradeoff. For TTFT-sensitive routes, we recommend small batch windows or prefix caching. For background jobs or exports, larger batching/quantization is fine.

[18:45] Priya: On security/residency: we need SOC2 type II, audit log details, customer-managed KMS possibility. Can you share docs?
[18:53] Aisha: Yes, we'll send SOC2 and a private deployment doc. That will be in the next steps. For the pilot we'll use Redwood Dedicated in us-west-2 with private networking options.

[21:30] Maya: Measurement specifics: what's the exact definition you'll record for TTFT? Are you including network transfer time to client or just server-side?
[21:38] Liam: We'll do both. Primary SLO will be server-side TTFT (receive timestamp to first token emitted on server), and we'll also record end-to-end (client-observed) where possible. For TPOT it's server-side generation end-to-end, plus a per-token microstat to compute per-token latency (ms/token).

[23:44] Oliver: Sampling windows and retention — we'll want samples retained for 90 days and dashboards.
[23:50] Aisha: Redwood Console can retain per-route stats; for pilot we'll retain 30 days by default but can enable 90 days as an add-on — we will include a demo of dashboards in the next call.

[26:12] Liam: Example SLO table we're proposing in the pilot charter (spoken):
- TTFT (short <=50 tokens): p95 <= 300ms, p99 <= 700ms
- TTFT (medium 51-200): p95 <= 420ms, p99 <= 1.2s
- TPOT (median 45 tokens): p95 <= 1.8s, p99 <= 5s
Those numbers are starting points; we'll tune after the dry-run.

[28:02] Maya: For long summaries (600 tokens) what's a realistic TPOT?
[28:07] Liam: Depends on model and decoding. If you're streaming, users perceive progress earlier. But total time might be 12–20s unoptimized; quantization and batching can drop that. For POC we treat long outputs as a separate bucket and set relaxed SLOs.

[30:18] Jon: OK about the sampling and test harness — what tooling will you use? JMeter? Locust?
[30:24] Liam: We typically use a combination of a custom JMeter/locust harness wrapped with our request wrapper to simulate concurrency and injection of KV cache hit/miss patterns. We'll provide config and also a small harness that replays sanitized production traces.

[32:45] Maya: On measurement metrics please also include failure modes: increased latency when fallback to smaller model happens, error budget burn metric, and downstream retry amplification.
[32:55] Liam: Agreed — we'll capture model fallback counts, rate of rate-limited responses, 5xx rates, and compute error budget burn using standard SRE formulas.

[35:10] Oliver: Timeline? We need a pilot done in 6 weeks to present to the board. Is that feasible?
[35:16] Aisha: Rough plan — week 0 (this week) collect traffic and security docs; week 1 Redwood dry-run on staging; week 2 sandbox canary + small fixups; week 3 run full canary and measurement; week 4 analyze and produce SLO report. That hits ~4 weeks but allow 6 as buffer.

[37:40] Jon: How will you handle KV cache warm-up? We have many repeated prefixes in chat.
[37:46] Liam: We'll run a warm-up phase that replays recent prefixes to populate the KV and measure hit-rate. We'll also instrument cache hit-rate; a common target is >60% hit rate for chat flows to get TTFT improvements.

[39:58] Maya: Are there any known gotchas about measuring p99 in bursty traffic?
[40:03] Liam: Yes — momentary infra noise and cold starts can skew p99. That's why we run synthetic bursts and multiple windows and compare server-side vs client-side. Also consider burn-in to reduce cold starts. We'll also include warm vs cold sample classification in the report.

[42:20] Aisha: Quick recap: agreed initial SLO bands (short/medium TPFT/TPOT), traffic profile to collect (7-day logs), test harness and runbook to be shared, security docs to be sent, and canary scheduling. Next call we'll review dry-run results.

[42:45] Priya: Please include a high-level data flow diagram for the Dedicated setup showing KMS, VPC peering.
[42:52] Aisha: We'll include that.

[44:30] Oliver: One more: cost approximation — do you have a per-1000-token estimate for the pilot with quantization?
[44:36] Liam: We can provide a rough estimate once we have token distribution. But rough ballpark on Dedicated optimized runs might be 0.6–1.2 USD per 1k tokens depending on model/quantization. We'll provide a clearer number in the pricing doc.

[46:55] Jon: For acceptance criteria: if TTFT p95 improves by 20% over our baseline and TPOT p95 is within your proposed bucket, we mark pilot success?
[47:03] Aisha: Sounds good — we'll also include reliability (error rates <0.1%) and no data residency issues.

[49:10] Maya: I'll get the logs and a pointer to the schema; we may need to mask PII.
[49:17] Aisha: Understood — we only need sanitized traces for the harness.

[50:00] Jordan: Quick note — I'll add the next steps and action items to the CRM and share the calendar invites for the canary prep slot.
[50:08] Aisha: Thanks all, we'll follow up via email and drop the benchmark template.
[50:14] Oliver: Great talk, thanks.
[50:16] Meeting ended.
